Look for the math

Jefferson's was the first apportionment method used by the US Congress. It always rounds down — and uses a smaller divisor to make the seats add up.

Lowering the divisor

The standard divisor divides the total population by the number of seats. Rounding all quotas down usually leaves seats unassigned, so Jefferson's method decreases the divisor until the floors add exactly to the house size. Equivalently, each next seat goes to the state with the largest population / (seats + 1), the D'Hondt priority.

What the check found

The logic test examines nearly two thousand random countries: every allocation fills the house, the priority rule matches an independent transcription, the divisor's floors agree with the allocation (up to a one-seat tie), and the results match the Jefferson column of the site's combined apportionment calculator.
